scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance dates back to the pre-colonial era of the Bunyoro and Tooro kingdoms.
It originated as a social and ceremonial practice where young people gathered under the moonlight to socialize and compete for partners.
Historically, it was a courtship contest where elders used the dance to select suitable husbands based on their physical endurance.
on_screen: Map: Uganda · Africa
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Beyond courtship, Entogoro is performed during weddings, initiation rites, and Empaako naming ceremonies.
It symbolizes cultural identity, physical prowess, and the social expectations of marriage.
It serves as a tool for cultural education, passing down traditional knowledge to younger generations.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: NTOGORO DANCE (UGANDA) (https://archive.org/details/actonma-NTOGORO_DANCE_UGANDA)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers perform in groups of men (abakwongezi) and women (abakwetegerezi).
The movement involves energetic leg shaking by men to sound their rattles and graceful hip movements by women to accentuate their waist rings.
Formations include circles, lines, and pairs, with specific moments for individual improvisation such as spinning and jumping.
Watch for Ebinyege shaking, Entogoro swaying.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (KaVMSVIcD7c)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Moves between collective circles/lines and individual solo spots.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is accompanied by a master of ceremonies (omukama) who sings and chants.
Musical instruments include drums, which set the rhythmic patterns, as well as flutes and xylophones that provide melodic layers.
Listen for the Drums, Flutes, Xylophones, Ebinyege (leg rattles).
A dense percussive soundscape dominated by the sharp, dry rattling of gourds on the dancers' legs, underpinned by deep drum rhythms and punctuated by melodic flute and xylophone lines.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Male dancers wear shorts and shirts with dried gourd rattles (ebinyege) tied to their legs.
Female dancers wear long skirts and blouses with beaded or cowrie shell rings (entogoro) around their waists.
Performances traditionally took place outdoors in community spaces, but are now common on formal stages and at cultural festivals.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The performance is led by the omukama (master of ceremonies), who directs the dancers and audience.
Ethnomusicologist Linda Cimardi has documented the dance as a medium for staging local culture and negotiating gender expression in western Uganda.
The genre is a combination of Orunyege from Hoima and Fort Portal, which is more acrobatic, and Ntogoro from Masindi, which is noted for its grace and elegance.

Entogoro is a subclass of Ugandan folk dance, specifically belonging to the Batooro and Banyoro ethnic groups. it is part of the wider 'runyege' performance genre which includes music, dance, and acting.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Entogoro is sibling of Orunyege: The more acrobatic component of the combined Orunyege-Ntogoro genre.
Entogoro is same region of Baakisimba: Another major Ugandan traditional dance, though from the Baganda people.
